questions.prompt: A student says: 'I changed the drop height AND the marble mass to get clearer results.' What should you say?

choices.text: Good idea — more changes = clearer science
Problem — two IVs at once; you can't tell which caused the effect
Only wrong if the crater gets deeper

questions.explanation: One IV per test. Want both? Run two separate fair tests.
questions.science_idea: Confounding variables muddy the causal story.

questions.prompt: Testing if a heavier marble makes a deeper crater in sand. What is the independent variable (the one you change on purpose)?
questions.explanation: Independent = what you change. Dependent = crater depth (what you measure).
questions.science_idea: IV = change; DV = measure; controls = keep the same.

questions.prompt: Hypothesis: 'If plants are happier, then they grow taller because happiness helps.' What's weak here?

choices.text: 'Happier' isn't measurable; IV needs a clear, measurable change

questions.explanation: Replace 'happier' with something measurable (hours of light, ml of water, etc.).

questions.prompt: Same mass, different drop heights. Higher drop → deeper crater. What changed, and why deeper?

choices.text: Height → more speed → more kinetic energy
Nothing about energy; sand just got softer

questions.explanation: Higher drop → more gravitational potential energy → converts to more speed/KE.
questions.science_idea: GPE → KE as the object falls.

questions.prompt: Why do scientists often repeat a measurement several times?

choices.text: To spot odd results and see if the pattern is reliable
To change more variables each time
Repeats replace the need for control variables

questions.explanation: Repeats improve reliability; they don't replace keeping controls constant.
questions.science_idea: Reliability ≠ fair test — you need both.
